newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU clears new German regional aid plan.
newsitem.headline: EU clears new German regional aid plan.

text.p: After months of hard bargaining with Germany, the European Commission cleared a plan on Wednesday which will allow Bonn to continue pouring huge subsidies into its regions over the next three years.

But the agreement keeps state subsidies paid in the former West Germany at their current level despite a long and fierce battle by German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt to increase it to match huge subsidies in the east.

"Currently, between 66 to 67 percent of European Union regions benefit from some sort of support or another. That is why we had to fight against an extension (of the regions getting aid)," European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert told a news conference.
The Commission's statement on the new German regional aid scheme for 1997-1999 does not say how much money Germany will spend to help develop regions hit by high unemployment.

But Commission officials said earlier this week that it would amount to as much as seven billion European currency units ($8.68 billion), of which 90 percent would benefit the regions under communist rule until 1990.

The Commission's decision effectively allows the former East Germany to keep the statute of "supported regions" and extends that concept to the whole of Berlin -- therefore ending the distinction previously made between the city's east and west inherited from the Cold War period.
It kept subsidies paid in the western regions within the existing level measured in terms of aided population.
Rexrodt had asked EU permission to help as much as 22 percent of the population in west Germany, but the Commission insisted that aid should remain below the current 20.8 percent level.
"There has been a lot of arm wrestling over this," one source said.

To be eligible for aid, a region must suffer from high unemployment and have a gross domestic product below the national average. Although this is undisputed as far as east Germany is concerned, many western regions included in the scheme appear to fail both tests, the sources told Reuters.
The huge level of subsidies being granted in Germany has met opposition not only from the Commission but also from other EU states.

The 1997-1999 scheme will be paid out of German, not EU coffers, although the Union will also contribute to regional development in Germany through its structural funds as it does for other European regions.
